name: Chiropractic adjustments

lead: A chiropractic adjustment is a quick manual thrust applied to spinal joints. People seek it for back and neck discomfort and some hope it straightens the spine for better posture and frame.

The chain is manipulated spinal joints, reduced stiffness or discomfort, then easier upright posture. Reviews summarized on Wikipedia report modest or low-certainty benefits for some back and neck pain and no good evidence for non-musculoskeletal conditions. No study was found testing lasting posture or appearance change.

paras: A licensed chiropractor applies a high-velocity, low-amplitude thrust to a joint, often over a series of visits and sometimes alongside exercises or stretches. Chiropractic theory attributes effects to correcting subluxations, a concept described as unsubstantiated.

Soreness and headache are common and temporary. Rare serious events, including stroke after neck manipulation, are reported, and causality is debated. The profession is licensed in most places; people with neck pain, bone conditions or on blood thinners may want to discuss it with a doctor first.

angle.text: People seek chiropractic adjustments hoping to ease spinal stiffness and straighten posture and frame. The path runs from manipulated joints to less stiffness to easier upright posture. Trials have looked at back and neck pain with low-certainty benefit; lasting posture change has not been shown.

lead: A chiropractic adjustment is a manual intervention, most often a high-velocity, low-amplitude thrust, applied to the joints of the spine; chiropractors use "adjustment" for what clinical literature calls spinal manipulation [1][2]. It is the core technique of chiropractic, a profession founded in the 1890s by D. D. Palmer [2].

It is most often used for back and neck pain. In appearance and posture communities it is discussed as a way to correct alignment or "reset" the spine. Reviews summarized on Wikipedia report modest or low-certainty benefits for some back and neck pain and no good evidence for non-musculoskeletal conditions, while safety discussions centre on rare serious events after neck manipulation [1][2].
infobox: Diversified, Activator, Gonstead, Thompson, Cox flexion-distraction
Licensed profession; rules vary by country

paras: Adjustments are delivered by hand or with instruments such as the Activator. Common schools include Diversified (the most widely used), Activator, Gonstead, Thompson, Cox flexion-distraction and Sacro-Occipital Technique [2]. Chiropractors also give ergonomic and postural advice and exercise guidance [2].

Spinal manipulation has roots in bone-setting and ancient medicine, and its modern revival began in late 19th-century North America [1]. Palmer's subluxation theory held that spinal misalignments affect nervous function and general health; Wikipedia describes the concept as unsubstantiated [1][2]. Chiropractors divide into "straights" who keep the original philosophy and "mixers" who blend in science [2]. The American Medical Association called chiropractic an "unscientific cult" in 1966 and boycotted it until losing an antitrust case in 1987 [2].

For low back pain, a 2012 Cochrane review cited on Wikipedia found manipulation no more effective than placebo for acute pain, while a 2019 meta-analysis found results comparable to recommended treatments for chronic pain; a 2017 American College of Physicians guideline cited low-quality evidence [1]. For neck pain, a 2015 Cochrane review found no high-quality evidence, with low-to-moderate quality evidence that several sessions may relieve pain compared with some medications [1]. A 2019 review found no evidence of benefit for non-musculoskeletal conditions such as asthma or migraine [1]. A 2011 critical review of 45 systematic reviews concluded spinal manipulation had not been convincingly shown effective for any condition [2].

A 1987 pilot study of nine patients with sacroiliac dysfunction used a force platform to measure gait symmetry before and after chiropractic manipulation [3]. No controlled study was found testing adjustments for aesthetic posture or facial appearance outcomes.

Mild temporary effects such as soreness, headache and fatigue are common, estimated at 33 to 61 percent of patients [2]. Rare serious events, including stroke from vertebral artery dissection, have been associated mainly with neck manipulation, and causality is disputed [1][2]. A 2001 Ontario case-control study found vertebrobasilar stroke was associated with chiropractic visits in people under 45 [4]. A 2008 population-based study compared chiropractic and primary care visits, since neck pain and headache are themselves early symptoms of dissection [5]. Underreporting makes incidence difficult to estimate [1][2].

A US national survey report tracked the use of yoga, meditation and chiropractors among adults [6]. Chiropractors in the US hold a Doctor of Chiropractic degree and are licensed by state; in the UK the General Chiropractic Council regulates the profession [2]. Skeptical consumer-health critics caution about full-spine X-rays and non-musculoskeletal claims [2].
